opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different ways to think about the cost here, and it depends a lot on what exactly you mean by "looping."

The simplest version is something like: instead of the model emitting a token and then reading that token back in, you take some late-layer activation and feed it back into an earlier layer, so the model can do more serial computation in a continuous, high-dimensional space rather than bottlenecking everything through discrete tokens. In terms of raw inference FLOPs, that's not necessarily more expensive than chain-of-thought. A forward pass through some number of layers costs roughly the same whether the input is a token embedding or a recycled activation. So if you're doing, say, a thousand steps of looped reasoning versus a thousand tokens of chain-of-thought, the inference compute is in the same ballpark.

The real costs show up in training. With normal chain-of-thought, a lot of the training is parallelizable. You can do teacher forcing: you have the whole sequence, and you compute the loss on every position at once. That's a huge part of why transformers won out over RNNs in the first place. Once you have recurrence in activation space, you lose a lot of that. To train the model to use the loop well, you need to actually unroll it, backpropagate through many serial steps, and deal with all the classic RNN problems: memory costs from storing activations across the unroll, vanishing or exploding gradients, instability. You can use tricks like truncated backprop or only training on a limited number of loop iterations, but those come with their own downsides, and it's not obvious you get the full benefit.

There's also a reinforcement learning angle. A lot of where reasoning ability comes from now is RL on chain-of-thought, and that's already fairly serial and expensive because you have to generate rollouts. Looping doesn't make that dramatically worse in principle, but you lose some of the nice properties. With text, you can bootstrap from pretraining: the model already knows how to write reasoning in English, so RL is shaping a prior that's already pretty good. With neuralese-style recurrence, you're kind of starting from scratch on what the internal language is, and it's not clear how much sample efficiency you give up.

So my overall take is: the inference cost isn't really the issue. The question is whether the training inefficiencies and engineering difficulties are outweighed by the gains from higher-bandwidth reasoning. Text tokens are a pretty narrow channel, something like a few bits to maybe a dozen-plus bits per token, while a residual stream activation carries vastly more information. That's a big potential advantage. My guess is that right now the costs dominate, which is why the frontier labs are mostly still doing text chain-of-thought, but I wouldn't be shocked if that flips over the next few years as people find better ways to train this stuff.

And from a safety perspective, that's something I watch pretty closely, because one of the nicest properties we currently have is that models' reasoning is mostly legible. If the efficiency gap closes and people move to opaque recurrent reasoning, we lose a lot of our ability to monitor what models are actually thinking, and I think that would be a pretty significant loss.

r001.rationale: It says looped inference is not necessarily more expensive and compares 1,000 loop steps with 1,000 chain-of-thought tokens as being in the same computational ballpark.

r002.rationale: It says training requires unrolling the loop and backpropagating through many serial steps, describing lost parallelism and additional training costs.

r003.rationale: It discusses serial computation in activation space but does not explain that applying looping while reading would make input-token processing sequential.

r004.rationale: It notes that chain-of-thought RL already requires expensive serial rollouts and says looping would not make that dramatically worse in principle.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a fair amount, because the naive version of it sounds very cheap and I think that's a bit misleading.

So the basic idea: right now, a transformer does one forward pass per token. Activations flow up through the layers once, you get a distribution over the next token, you sample, and you repeat. The only way the model gets more "thinking time" on a hard problem is by emitting more tokens — chain of thought, basically. The looping proposal is: instead of forcing the model to go through the bottleneck of writing a token, let it take the residual stream at the top and feed it back into the bottom, or into some middle block, and run through again. Multiple internal passes per output token. Sometimes people call this recurrence, or "latent reasoning," or universal-transformer-style stuff.

The first-order cost is pretty simple. If you loop the whole stack K times, you're paying roughly K times the compute per token. If you loop only a chunk — say the middle third of the layers — then you're paying something like one plus K times a third. That part is easy to estimate, and it's really just the same math as a bigger model, because in terms of FLOPs, a looped model is basically a deeper model with tied weights.

The thing that's less obvious is that compute is not really the binding constraint in a lot of these settings — it's memory and the shape of the computation. In inference, you're usually bottlenecked on memory bandwidth, moving the weights through the chip, rather than on raw FLOPs. And looping is actually kind of nice there, because you reuse the same weights, so your weight traffic goes down relative to a model that's K times deeper with distinct parameters. On the other hand, the KV cache gets worse. If each loop iteration produces its own keys and values that later tokens attend to, you've multiplied your cache by K, and the cache is often the thing that actually limits how many sequences you can serve at once. So you can end up with a model that's cheap in FLOPs but expensive in the thing that matters.

Then there's training, which I think is where the real cost lives. Backprop through K iterations is backprop through K times as many layers, so you pay the compute, and you also pay memory to store activations for all of those steps unless you do something like checkpointing, which costs you compute again. And the thing that worries me more is that it's just harder to train. Deep recurrent computation has the classic issues — gradients that blow up or vanish over the loop — and the more iterations you want, the more you're fighting that. So you might find that in principle a 4x looped model is as expressive as a 4x deeper model, but in practice it trains to something noticeably worse per FLOP, and now the "cost" is really a hit to your scaling efficiency rather than a clean multiplier.

The way I'd actually assess it, if someone asked me to be concrete: I'd ask what you're comparing against. The honest baseline isn't "same model, no loop." It's "same total compute, spent some other way." You could make the model deeper with untied weights, you could make it wider, or you could just let it do more chain of thought. And chain of thought is the one that's interesting, because it already gives you adaptive compute — the model thinks longer on hard problems and shorter on easy ones — and it's trivially cheap to implement, and it's legible. You can read it.

That last point is kind of my actual view on this. I think a lot of the appeal of looping is "the model can reason without the tokens," and from a capability perspective, maybe you get something out of that — the model can carry a richer representation around than it can squeeze into a word. But from a safety perspective that's precisely the thing I'd rather not have. If the model's doing a bunch of serial reasoning in the residual stream where I can't see it, I've lost one of the most useful handles I have. So when I assess the cost I sort of mentally add a line item for that, even though it's not a FLOP.

And then the empirical question of whether you get a real win — I think the evidence so far is kind of mixed. There are results showing you can get a somewhat better perplexity per parameter, which makes sense, you're reusing parameters. There's less clear evidence that you get better results per FLOP, which is what actually matters at scale. And there's pretty limited evidence that it gives you qualitatively new reasoning ability that you couldn't have gotten from chain of thought or just scaling. My prior is that it's maybe a modest efficiency gain in some regimes and not the architectural step change people sometimes talk about it as. But I'd want to see someone run the scaling laws carefully before I was confident either way.

r002.rationale: It states that backpropagation through K iterations incurs the compute of K times as many layers.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the cost of running the model from the cost of getting it to use that computation effectively. If you take a transformer and loop its activations through the same layers several times, each pass still costs compute. Reusing the weights doesn’t make those additional passes free. But it does let you spend more computation without increasing the number of parameters, which can be a useful tradeoff.

The relevant comparison is often with having the model generate a chain of thought. That also spends additional compute on reasoning, so looping isn’t necessarily more expensive for a given level of performance. You’re just allocating the computation differently. Whether it’s actually more efficient depends on how much useful reasoning the model learns to do in each pass.

And that’s the part I’d be uncertain about. It’s relatively straightforward to specify an architecture that loops; it’s harder to know what training procedure will make those loops useful, and whether the resulting model will outperform spending the same compute on a more conventional approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is the cost per step from the number of steps you need to get a good answer. If you take a transformer and run its activations through the same layers multiple times, those extra passes aren’t free. Roughly speaking, twice as many passes means twice as much compute for that part of the model. Sharing the weights can save memory, but it doesn’t eliminate the computation.

The interesting question is whether those passes are a more efficient way to do reasoning than generating additional tokens. With tokens, you’re repeatedly running the model, but you get an explicit scratchpad that later steps can attend to. With internal recurrence, you could potentially avoid some of that overhead and represent intermediate work more compactly. But you might also have a harder time training the model to use those intermediate states effectively.

So I wouldn’t assume that looping is either prohibitively expensive or an obvious computational win. You’d want to compare the performance you get at a fixed training and inference budget, including against a model that just spends more tokens thinking. The number of loops alone doesn’t tell you which approach is better.
